figures.caption: Isolated Spread Footing
figures.description: Introduction General classification and definition of shallow foundations for all design applications. Shallow foundation generally defined as bearing depth less than about 2 times the foundation width Understanding theoretical assumptions behind design procedures is more important than the strict definition Bearing capacity equations have theoretical limitations that vary as a function of depth Common types illustrated in Figures 2-1 through 2-5 Isolated Spread Footings Single column support where loads can be distributed to adequate bearing material through an individual footing. Designed to distribute concentrated column loads and prevent shear failure of bearing material Typical minimum size for bridge columns is 3 m x 3 m (10 ft x 10 ft) Footing size increases with eccentric loads

figures.caption: Spill-Through Abutment on Combination Strip Footing
figures.description: Combination Footings Multiple-column support where individual footings would overlap or where non-uniform column spacing or large overturning moments are present. Support two or more columns on a single rectangular or trapezoidal footing Used when column spacing is non-uniform or when isolated footings would overlap Spill-through abutments are a bridge application of combination footings (Figure 2-6) Frame action allows resistance to large overturning or rotational moments Spill-through abutments used at stream crossings to place foundations below scour level Design choice depends on available space, load distribution, soil variability, and economics

figures.caption: Typical Mat Foundation
figures.description: Mat Foundations Structures where spread footings would cover more than 50% of the plan area, or where differential settlement must be minimized over weak or variable ground conditions. Single heavily reinforced concrete slab underlying the entire structure or major portion Economical when spread footings would cover more than about 50% of the plan area (Peck et al. 1974) Principal advantage is ability to bridge over soft spots and reduce differential movement Suitable for relatively weak soils or lightweight structures Limited applicability for bridge support; applicable for bascule piers and movable bridge supports Common transportation applications include maintenance facilities, storage bins, and box culverts Large mat foundation design discussed in Section 8.6

figures.caption: Note that the allowable bearing capacity of a footing is controlled by shear-failure
figures.description: Allowable Bearing Capacity Conceptual framework for all shallow foundation bearing capacity evaluation. Allowable bearing capacity combines shear failure prevention and settlement limitation For narrow footings, shear failure controls; for wide footings, settlement controls Footing width B is the key design variable for both criteria As B increases, factor of safety against shear failure increases but settlement potential also increases The depth of influence increases proportionally with footing width

figures.description: Footings on Cohesionless Soils Settlement estimation for footings on sands, gravels, and non-plastic silts. Settlement typically controls design of footings on cohesionless soils rather than bearing capacity Hough method is RECOMMENDED as primary design tool - conservative, reliable, easy to implement Hough method overpredicts settlement by factor of ~2 (s_o = 0.82 from Gifford study, s_o = 0.53 from load tests) D'Appolonia method is most statistically accurate (s_o = 0.51) but may underpredict by factor of 0.77 Both methods use SPT N-values as primary input Load-settlement curve method (Briaud) using pressuremeter is promising alternate

figures.caption: Corrected SPT (N) versus Overburden Pressure (after Liao & Whitman, 1986)
figures.description: Hough Method Primary recommended method for settlement estimation on normally consolidated cohesionless soils. Applicable ONLY for normally consolidated cohesionless soils Uses SPT N-values corrected for overburden stress (Liao & Whitman, 1986) Overburden correction: N'/N = 1/(sigma'_vo/95.76)^0.5, maximum 2.0, sigma'_vo in kPa Bearing capacity index C' obtained from Figure 5-19 based on corrected N' and soil type Profile subdivided into ~3-m layers to depth of ~3*B_f Settlement computed layer-by-layer using Equation 5-24 and summed Figure 5-19 has curves for: clean uniform medium sand, well graded silty sand & gravel, clean well graded fine to coarse sand, sandy clay, inorganic silt

figures.caption: Keys are typically difficult to construct while maintaining the
figures.description: Sliding and Lateral Stability All shallow foundations subjected to lateral loads; minimum FS = 1.5 against sliding for bridge foundations. Passive earth pressure resistance is conservatively IGNORED in most shallow foundation designs Sliding resistance on granular soil: F_R = (W + P_v) * tan(delta), where delta = friction angle at interface For concrete cast against granular soil: tan(delta) = tan(phi) of the soil Sliding resistance on clay: F_R = c_a * B_f, where c_a ~ c_u (undrained shear strength) Minimum FS against sliding = 1.5 for bridge foundations Do NOT combine drained (Eq 5-38) and undrained (Eq 5-39) sliding resistance Keys in cohesive soils/soft rock can add resistance (Eq 5-41); keys in granular soils mainly increase shear surface length Table 5-15 provides friction factors

figures.caption: Global Slope Stability with Respect to Shallow Foundation Locations
figures.description: Global Stability All shallow foundations near slopes or on ground with non-level geometry. Evaluate global stability when ground geometry near the footing invalidates bearing capacity theory assumptions Footing loads can either stabilize or destabilize a slope depending on location (Figure 5-23) Use limit equilibrium methods (Bishop or Spencer method of slices) to check global stability Detailed slope stability guidance is in the Soils and Foundation Workshop Reference Manual and TRB SR 247 Global stability check is separate from and additional to bearing capacity and settlement checks

figures.caption: Design Process Flow Chart – Bridge Shallow Foundation
figures.description: Design Process and Flow Chart Establishing the overall design workflow and discipline responsibilities for bridge shallow foundation design. 12-step design process with clear discipline assignments for each step Steps 1-3: Preliminary layout, geologic review, and site reconnaissance Step 4: Depth determination for scour and frost protection (hydraulic/geotechnical) Steps 5-6: Loads, settlement criteria, soil properties from exploration and lab testing Steps 7-9: Bearing capacity, sliding/passive resistance, global stability (geotechnical) Steps 10-12: Footing sizing, overturning/sliding checks, structural design (structural) Structural design (Step 12) uses factored loads and trapezoidal contact pressure, not the uniform equivalent pressure used for sizing

figures.caption: Coulomb Lateral Earth Pressure Definitions
figures.description: Active Pressure Distribution Computing active earth pressure coefficients for abutment design using Coulomb or Rankine theory. Coulomb active earth pressure coefficient (Equation 6-2) is the general case accounting for wall batter, backfill slope, and wall friction Rankine equation K_a = tan^2(45 - phi'/2) is the simplified case for vertical walls with level ground Rankine assumes no wall-soil friction; Coulomb includes interface friction angle delta Neither Coulomb nor Rankine basic equations account for surcharge or seismic loads Parameters: delta = wall/backfill friction angle, beta = backfill slope, theta = wall face inclination, phi' = soil friction angle

figures.caption: Lateral Earth Pressures on Abutments
figures.description: Live Load Surcharge Computing additional lateral load from traffic surcharge on abutment walls. Live load surcharge applies when traffic is within horizontal distance of 0.5H behind the wall If approach slab is present, live loads are applied to the corbel on the abutment backwall instead Equivalent surcharge height h_eq = 0.6 m (2 ft) with unit weight of 19.6 kN/m^3 (125 pcf) Surcharge pressure distribution is uniform along the wall, with resultant at H/2 from base P_LS = K * gamma' * h_eq * H

figures.description: Effective Footing Dimensions and Overturning Stability Computing effective footing dimensions for eccentric loading and checking overturning stability. Effective footing dimensions account for eccentric loading: B'_f = B_f - 2*e_B, L'_f = L_f - 2*e_L Eccentricity e = M / V (moment divided by vertical load) in each direction Effective area A' = B'_f * L'_f used for bearing stress calculation with uniform pressure assumption Eccentricity on soil must be < B/6 or L/6 to avoid zero contact pressure (AASHTO 1996) Eccentricity on rock must be < B/4 or L/4 If eccentricity within these limits, separate overturning calculation is not needed Effective dimensions are an approximation; structural design uses actual trapezoidal/triangular distributions

figures.description: Structural Design of the Footing Structural design of bridge spread footings using trapezoidal or triangular contact pressure distributions for reinforcement and shear checks. Assume rigid footing with linear contact pressure distribution (trapezoidal or triangular) For e_L <= L_f/6: trapezoidal distribution with q_max and q_min computed from Equations 6-9 and 6-10 For L_f/6 < e_L < L_f/2: triangular distribution with q_min = 0 and L_1 = 3[(L_f/2) - e_L] Use actual trapezoidal/triangular pressures for structural design, NOT the equivalent uniform pressure used for sizing Structural design per AASHTO Standard Specifications Section 8 Check: moment at column face, flexural steel in short direction, one-way shear at 'd' from column face, and punching (two-way) shear Abutment elements

figures.description: Mat Foundations Selection and design of mat foundations for buildings with high loads, poor soils, or erratic subsurface conditions.
